extracted.intended_audience: trial judges and litigators handling patent cases (Northern District of California model jury instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials providing definitions, legal standards, and jury-directed rules on claim construction, infringement (literal and equivalents), means-plus-function, burdens of proof, and related trial procedures tailored for the Northern District of California.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO (Patent and Trademark Office) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative branch of the U.S. Department of Commerce charged with overseeing and implementing the federal laws of patents and trademarks; responsible for examining all patent applications and issuing all patents in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain the agency that grants patents and conducts examination; appears in the glossary/definitions to orient jurors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously known subject matter in the field of a claimed invention for which a patent is being sought, including issued patents, publications, and knowledge deemed to be publicly available such as trade skills and trade practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines what materials/expertise an examiner considers when determining novelty/obviousness; later instructions rely on legal definitions of prior art when assessing validity and the doctrine of equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution History definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete written record of the proceedings in the PTO from the initial application to the issued patent, including office actions taken by the PTO and amendments filed by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies the documentary record that may inform claim meaning, prosecution history estoppel, or what the PTO considered during examination; becomes public upon patent issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reads On
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim 'reads on' a device or method when each required part (requirement) of the claim is found in the device or method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology used when comparing accused products/methods to claim requirements to determine literal infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention is 'reduced to practice' when it is sufficiently developed to show that it would work for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glossary definition relevant to issues of conception, invention date, and certain validity inquiries (e.g., prior art timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement (limitation) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A required part or step of an invention set forth in a patent claim; often used interchangeably with 'limitation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies vocabulary used throughout the instructions when referencing claim elements/limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A payment made to the owner of a patent by a nonowner in exchange for rights to make, use, or sell the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glossary term relevant to damages instructions (appears elsewhere in the instructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A required part of a patent application and an issued patent; a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the document that supports claims and discloses structure (important for means-plus-function analysis, written description/enablement issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: What a patent is and how one is obtained
rubrics_metrics.description: A United States patent gives the patent owner the right to prevent others from making, using, offering to sell, selling, or importing the patented invention in the U.S. during the patent term; to obtain a patent one must file an application with the PTO containing a specification and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains prosecution process: examiners review prior art, issue office actions, applicants can amend claims, and the resulting prosecution history becomes public; warns that a PTO grant does not preclude a court finding invalidity based on evidence not before the PTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent At Issue — court should show jury patent materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The court should show the jury the specification, drawings and claims including the claims at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical instruction to help jurors follow the evidence by making the patent documents available during trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of Contentions — jury's role and issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The court provides a summary of each party's positions; the jury must decide whether asserted claims have been infringed and whether those claims are invalid, and, if infringement and validity are found, determine money damages and willfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames the central factual and legal questions for jurors and clarifies that invalidity is a defense to infringement; includes admonition to keep an open mind and that willfulness is a separate finding that should not affect the damage award directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of proof (two standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two standards of proof apply depending on the issue: some issues require deciding whether something is 'more likely than not' (preponderance of the evidence), while other issues require deciding whether it is 'highly probable' (higher standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: to prove infringement the patent holder must persuade by a preponderance (more likely than not); to prove invalidity the accused infringer must persuade by a higher standard ('highly probable' / clear and convincing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction — judge's role
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deciding infringement or invalidity, the jury must understand the patent claims; it is the judge's job to explain the meaning of any claim language that needs interpretation, and the jury must accept those interpretations as correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court's claim interpretations should not be taken as an indication of the judge's views on infringement/invalidity; instructions must be coordinated with special instructions (e.g., means-plus-function). Authorities cited: Markman, Phillips, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement — burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove infringement of any claim, the patent holder must persuade the jury that it is more likely than not that the alleged infringer has infringed that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites authorities; reiterates the preponderance standard for infringement distinct from invalidity standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement — two-step process and claim-by-claim analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Deciding direct infringement involves (1) determining the meaning of the patent claim (claim construction) and (2) deciding whether the accused party has made, used, sold, offered for sale, or imported a product or method covered by a claim; each asserted claim must be considered individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: dependent claims include all requirements of their independent claim plus additional requirements (if independent not infringed, dependent cannot be infringed; if independent infringed, still evaluate dependent's additional requirements). Jurors must compare the accused product to the claims, not to plaintiff's commercial product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement — every claim requirement present
rubrics_metrics.description: A product or method literally infringes a claim if every requirement (limitation) of that claim is included in the product or method; if any requirement is missing, there is no literal infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains claim transition language: 'comprising' = open claim (extras allowed); 'consisting of' = closed (no other parts/steps allowed); 'consisting essentially of' = partially closed (extras allowed unless they materially affect basic and novel properties). Also explains that missing claim elements supplied by others do not establish liability unless the accused directed or controlled the other party (direction/control test); system claims may allow liability when parts operate in different places or times (Centillion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule against comparing accused product to plaintiff's commercial product
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding infringement, the jury may not compare the alleged infringer’s accused product or method to the patent holder’s commercial product or method; instead, the jury must compare the accused product or method to the claims of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures jurors focus on claim language as the boundary of protection rather than comparisons between competing products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents — equivalence test
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is no literal infringement, the jury must decide whether the accused product/method infringes under the doctrine of equivalents by determining whether the accused parts/steps are identical or equivalent to the claim requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A part/step is equivalent if persons of ordinary skill would think the differences were not substantial at the time of alleged infringement; one way to evaluate is the function-way-result test (performed substantially same function, in substantially same way, to achieve substantially same result). Known interchangeability at time of infringement may support equivalence but is not required. Doctrine cannot be used to cover subject matter that was in the prior art or would have been obvious, nor to recapture subject matter described but not claimed in the patent. Authorities: Warner-Jenkinson, Graver Tank, Festo, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on doctrine of equivalents (prior art and described-but-not-claimed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents cannot be used to find infringement if the subject matter alleged to be equivalent was in the prior art or would have been obvious, or if it was described in the patent but not claimed (unless sufficiently specific that one of ordinary skill would understand it was present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accused product is shown to be in the prior art, burden shifts to the patent holder to prove the asserted equivalents were not in the prior art or would not have been obvious. Cites Festo and related cases regarding limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-Plus-Function claims — scope and literal infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A means-plus-function requirement covers only the specific structure disclosed in the patent specification for performing the claimed function and the equivalents of those specific structures, not all possible structures that could perform the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court will identify the corresponding structure in the specification; to prove infringement the jury must find the accused product has structure that performs the claimed function (or equivalents). Example: 'means for processing data' is limited to structures disclosed in the spec and equivalents, not every possible data processing means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direction or control rule for combined/missing elements (joint performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: An accused infringer cannot be liable for infringement merely because other parties supplied missing elements, unless the accused specifically instructed or caused those parties to perform each step in an infringing manner (i.e., directed or controlled the acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies joint infringement/attribution standards and distinguishes ordinary business relationships from control sufficient to attribute steps to the accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: System claim attribution exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If one party controls and makes use of a system that contains all the requirements of the claim, that party may be an infringer even though the parts of the system do not all operate in the same place or at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate for system claims (not method claims); cites Centillion Data Sys. v. Qwest (Fed. Cir. 2011).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's claim interpretations do not indicate views on infringement/invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge's interpretation of claim language should not be taken as an indication that the judge has a view regarding issues such as infringement and invalidity; those issues remain for the jury to decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be read if claim constructions are handed out to jurors; reinforces neutrality of claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence format and trial procedure reminders
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening statements and closing arguments are not evidence; depositions read or played at trial are entitled to the same consideration as live testimony; keep an open mind until all evidence is heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural guidance to help jurors understand trial process and evaluation of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness finding separate from damages calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the jury decides infringement was willful, that decision should not affect any damage award the jury gives; the judge will take willfulness into account later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructs jurors to determine willfulness independently and not to modify damages based on willfulness in their award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove invalidity of any claim, the accused infringer must persuade the jury that it is highly probable that the claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals that invalidity carries a higher standard than infringement (i.e., clear and convincing evidence), and that the accused bears that burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent vs independent claims handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims include all requirements of a particular independent claim plus additional requirements; if an independent claim is not infringed, its dependent claims are not infringed; if the independent claim is infringed, the jury must still decide whether the dependent claim's additional requirements are infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides jurors on how to treat dependent claims in infringement analysis and avoid incorrect blanket conclusions.
